title: comptime `===` and `!==` compare containers by allocation identity and scalars by value, exactly as the same expressions do outside comptime
notes: guide/comptime.mdx:134 -- "The same function may be callable in both phases when its operations are valid in both"; reference/comptime.mdx:40 -- "Implicit evaluation must not change observable runtime semantics" (stated of implicit evaluation, and an explicit `comptime` that disagrees with runtime is the same hazard with the compiler asked for it); :74 (Allowed Inputs) -- comptime code may depend on "checked pure computation". Nothing in the specification sanctions structural equality, and the first sentence is the promise this case exists to hold: the answer an expression gives inside `comptime` is the answer it gives outside it. Both evaluators used to canonicalize each operand and compare the resulting JSON text, so `{ x: 1 } === { x: 1 }` and `[1] === [1]` were `true` at comptime and `false` at runtime, `!==` was inverted to match, and there was no diagnostic -- a fail-open whose wrong constant was folded into the emitted program. The sharpest form: one module can hold `comptime(sameRef)([1], [1])` next to `sameRef([1], [1])` and lower the first to `true` beside a second that is `false` at every execution. The corpus could not see any of it, because until this case no case spelled a container operand: every comptime equality expression compared strings, numbers, and booleans, which give the same answer under either relation. A cross-backend differential could not see it either -- both implementations copied the same wrong operation, so they agreed with each other while disagreeing with JavaScript -- which is why every value here is asserted directly against the JavaScript answer rather than by comparing the backends. The rule pinned is not "never canonicalize": scalars compare by value, containers compare by retained allocation identity, and canonical serialization does not participate in equality at all -- it answers "do these print the same?", not "are these the same value?", and stays correct for `JSON.stringify`, the emitted result, and digests. The first line walks the containers: alias, distinct twin, and both under `===` and `!==` (the four semantic forms), then identity preserved through a property read, then `slice()` as a copy that must NOT be identical, then an object against an array. The second line pins the operations that were already right, so a future refactor cannot "fix" them into identity comparisons: scalar `===`/`!==` by value, and `indexOf`/`includes`, whose JavaScript definition is strict equality and which now route through the same primitive rather than through canonical text. One strict-equality primitive per evaluator now owns the relation: `strictEquals` in poc/src/build/comptime-intrinsic.ts and `ctStrictEquals` in compiler/forkbridge/comptime.go.txt, the latter comparing `*ctArrayData` / `*ctObjectData` pointers -- the container pointers the fork was already retaining for exactly this purpose.
